subject: social_science
chapter_title: The Making of the National Movement: 1870s-1947

concepts.title: The Emergence of Nationalism and Early Political Associations
concepts.definition: The development of a shared consciousness among Indians that India belonged to all its people, leading to the formation of political associations to challenge British control over the nation's resources.
concepts.key_idea: The realization that India's resources and systems belonged to its diverse population, not the British rulers.
question_patterns: What factors led to the emergence of nationalism in India in the late nineteenth century?
Which early political associations were formed in the 1870s and 1880s to represent Indian interests?
How did the concept of sovereignty shape the goals of early political organizations?
Explain the significance of the term sarvajanik in the context of the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha.
Why did the educated elite form political associations after 1850?

solution_steps.action: Identify early political associations
solution_steps.explain: Recognize organizations like Poona Sarvajanik Sabha, Indian Association, Madras Mahajan Sabha, and Bombay Presidency Association formed in the 1870s and 1880s.

solution_steps.action: Explain the concept of sovereignty
solution_steps.explain: Understand that these groups operated under the modern democratic principle that Indian people should be empowered to manage their own affairs independently.

concepts.title: British Repressive Measures of the 1870s and 1880s
concepts.definition: A series of legislative acts passed by the British administration, including the Arms Act and Vernacular Press Act, which restricted Indian freedoms and fueled national discontent.
concepts.key_idea: Repressive British laws like the Arms Act, Vernacular Press Act, and the withdrawal of the Ilbert Bill intensified Indian dissatisfaction.
question_patterns: Why were people dissatisfied with British rule in the 1870s and 1880s?
What was the purpose of the Vernacular Press Act of 1878?
How did the Arms Act of 1878 restrict the rights of Indian citizens?
Explain the controversy surrounding the introduction and withdrawal of the Ilbert Bill in 1883.
How did British legislative actions in the late nineteenth century highlight racial discrimination?

solution_steps.action: Analyze the Arms Act and Vernacular Press Act of 1878
solution_steps.explain: The Arms Act prevented Indians from owning weapons, while the Vernacular Press Act allowed the government to seize newspaper assets to silence critics.

solution_steps.action: Analyze the Ilbert Bill controversy of 1883
solution_steps.explain: The bill sought equality by allowing Indian judges to try Europeans, but white opposition forced its withdrawal, exposing British racial bias.

concepts.title: Establishment of the Indian National Congress
concepts.definition: The formation of an all-India political organization in December 1885 at Bombay, bringing together representatives from different regions to voice national demands.
concepts.key_idea: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 by 72 delegates to provide a unified platform for educated Indians.
question_patterns: When and where was the Indian National Congress established?
Who were the prominent early leaders of the Indian National Congress?
What role did A.O. Hume play in the formation of the Congress?
Who did the Indian National Congress seek to speak for during its inception?
How did early newspapers and leaders describe the purpose of the first National Congress?

solution_steps.action: Identify the founding details of the Congress
solution_steps.explain: The Congress was established in December 1885 when 72 delegates met in Bombay under early leaders like Dadabhai Naoroji and W.C. Bonnerji, with help from retired official A.O. Hume.

solution_steps.action: Define the representative character of the Congress
solution_steps.explain: As stated by Badruddin Tyabji, the Congress aimed to represent all communities and classes of India, not just any single group.

concepts.title: Moderate Phase of the Congress
concepts.definition: The initial twenty years of the Indian National Congress characterized by peaceful methods, constitutional demands, and raising awareness about the economic drain of India.
concepts.key_idea: Moderates sought administrative reforms, greater representation, and highlighted the economic ruin caused by British rule.
question_patterns: Who were the Moderates and what were their main objectives?
What administrative reforms did the early Congress demand from the British?
How did the Moderates criticize the economic impact of British rule?
Why did the Moderates demand the Indianisation of the administration?
What methods did Moderate leaders use to develop public awareness about British rule?

solution_steps.action: Identify Moderate objectives and demands
solution_steps.explain: Moderates demanded greater representation in legislative councils, civil service exams in India, separation of the judiciary from the executive, and repeal of the Arms Act.

solution_steps.action: Explain the economic critique and methods
solution_steps.explain: They highlighted how British rule caused poverty and famines through high land revenue and drain of wealth, using newspapers, articles, and speeches to mobilize public opinion.

concepts.title: The Rise of Radical Politics and the Partition of Bengal
concepts.definition: The emergence of a more assertive leadership within the Congress that advocated self-reliance, opposed the 1905 partition of Bengal, and initiated the Swadeshi movement.
concepts.key_idea: Radicals like Lal-Bal-Pal rejected the 'politics of prayers' and led the mass protest against the partition of Bengal.
question_patterns: How did the political style of the Radicals differ from that of the Moderates?
Why did Viceroy Curzon partition Bengal in 1905?
What was the Swadeshi movement and where was it strongest?
Explain the slogan 'Freedom is my birthright and I shall have it' and who raised it.
What motives did the British have behind splitting Bengal?

solution_steps.action: Contrast Radicals with Moderates
solution_steps.explain: Radicals like Bepin Chandra Pal, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and Lala Lajpat Rai criticized the Moderates' 'politics of prayers' and emphasized self-reliance and mass struggle.

solution_steps.action: Examine the Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi Movement
solution_steps.explain: Viceroy Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905 to curtail Bengali political influence. This sparked the Swadeshi movement, which promoted self-help, national education, and boycott of British goods.

concepts.title: Early Twentieth Century Political Developments and Splits
concepts.definition: Key political events between 1906 and 1916, including the formation of the Muslim League, the Surat split of the Congress, and their subsequent reunion and alliance.
concepts.key_idea: The formation of the Muslim League, the 1907 Congress split, and the 1916 Lucknow Pact shaped early nationalist alignments.
question_patterns: When and where was the All India Muslim League formed?
What were the main demands of the Muslim League in its early years?
Why did the Congress split in 1907 and when did it reunite?
What was the significance of the Lucknow Pact of 1916?
How did separate electorates affect communal politics after 1909?

solution_steps.action: Trace the formation of the Muslim League and separate electorates
solution_steps.explain: The Muslim League was formed in Dacca in 1906, supporting partition and demanding separate electorates, which the British conceded in 1909.

solution_steps.action: Explain the Congress split and the Lucknow Pact
solution_steps.explain: The Congress split in 1907 over the use of boycott, reunited in 1915, and signed the Lucknow Pact with the Muslim League in 1916 to work together for representative government.

concepts.title: Economic and Political Impact of the First World War
concepts.definition: The profound changes brought by the global conflict of 1914-1918, which altered India's economic landscape, expanded local industries, and created widespread discontent.
concepts.key_idea: The First World War led to high taxes, rising prices, industrial expansion, and a new anti-colonial consciousness among returning soldiers.
question_patterns: What economic impact did the First World War have on India?
How did the First World War benefit Indian business groups?
Why did the recruitment of soldiers during the First World War cause resentment in villages?
How did the Russian Revolution of 1917 inspire Indian nationalists?
In what ways did the First World War alter the political situation in India?

solution_steps.action: Analyze economic consequences of the war
solution_steps.explain: The war caused a massive rise in British defense expenditure, leading to increased taxes, high inflation, and severe hardships for common people, while Indian industries expanded due to reduced imports.

solution_steps.action: Analyze political consequences of the war
solution_steps.explain: Forced recruitment of soldiers created rural anger, while returning soldiers shared insights on imperialist exploitation. The 1917 Russian Revolution also spread socialist ideas.

concepts.title: The Advent of Mahatma Gandhi and Early Satyagrahas
concepts.definition: The return of Mahatma Gandhi from South Africa in 1915 and his initial localized non-violent struggles in Champaran, Kheda, and Ahmedabad.
concepts.key_idea: Gandhiji emerged as a respected leader, applying non-violent satyagraha to local peasant and worker grievances.
question_patterns: When did Mahatma Gandhi return to India and from where?
What were Gandhiji's earliest local interventions in India?
How did Gandhiji's experience in South Africa prepare him for leadership in India?
Explain the significance of the Ahmedabad millworkers' strike of 1918.
Who were the key leaders Gandhiji connected with during his early local movements?

solution_steps.action: Identify Gandhi's return and background
solution_steps.explain: Gandhiji arrived in India in 1915 from South Africa, where he had led successful non-violent struggles against racial discrimination.

solution_steps.action: Outline early local campaigns
solution_steps.explain: He spent his first year traveling, then led localized movements in Champaran, Kheda, and the successful Ahmedabad millworkers' strike in 1918.

concepts.title: The Rowlatt Satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh Massacre
concepts.definition: The first nation-wide protest campaign launched by Gandhiji in 1919 against repressive British legislation, which was met with brutal state violence in Amritsar.
concepts.key_idea: The Rowlatt Satyagraha was a unified struggle against the curbing of basic freedoms, marked by the tragic Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
question_patterns: Why did Gandhiji call for a satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act in 1919?
How did the Indian public respond to the Rowlatt Act?
What were the Jallianwala Bagh atrocities and who was responsible for them?
Why did Rabindranath Tagore renounce his knighthood?
How did the Rowlatt Satyagraha foster Hindu-Muslim unity?

solution_steps.action: Explain the Rowlatt Act and the satyagraha call
solution_steps.explain: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 restricted freedom of expression and enhanced police powers. Gandhiji called for a national hartal on 6 April 1919.

solution_steps.action: Describe the British repression and Jallianwala Bagh
solution_steps.explain: On 13 April 1919, General Dyer opened fire on a peaceful gathering at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar. In protest of these atrocities, Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood.

concepts.title: The Khilafat Agitation and Non-Cooperation Movement
concepts.section: Khilafat agitation and the Non-Cooperation Movement
concepts.definition: A major joint mass movement launched in 1920 combining Muslim anger over the treatment of the Turkish Khalifa with Indian demands for Swaraj and justice for Punjab wrongs.
concepts.key_idea: The alliance of the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements created unprecedented Hindu-Muslim unity and mass mobilization.
question_patterns: What was the Khilafat agitation and who were its main leaders?
Why did Gandhiji support the Khilafat movement?
What methods were adopted during the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1921-22?
How did the Non-Cooperation Movement affect the import of foreign cloth?
What was the connection between the Khilafat issue and the demand for Swaraj?

solution_steps.action: Explain the origins of the Khilafat movement
solution_steps.explain: Indian Muslims, led by Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali, protested the harsh treaty imposed on the Turkish Khalifa by the British after World War I.

solution_steps.action: Describe the course of the Non-Cooperation Movement
solution_steps.explain: Gandhiji merged the Khilafat protest with the demand for Swaraj. People boycotted schools, courts, and foreign goods, and lit bonfires of foreign cloth.

concepts.title: People's Initiatives and Local Interpretations of Satyagraha
concepts.definition: The diverse ways in which different social classes, peasants, and tribals interpreted Gandhiji's message to address their own local grievances, sometimes deviating from non-violence.
concepts.key_idea: Ordinary people often viewed Gandhiji as a messiah and linked his name to local struggles against landlords and forest laws.
question_patterns: How did different groups of people interpret Gandhiji's call for Non-Cooperation?
What were the forest satyagrahas in Guntur and why were they organized?
How did the peasants of Pratapgarh use Gandhiji's name to stop illegal evictions?
What actions did tea garden labourers in Assam take in the name of Gandhi?
Why did some popular initiatives not conform to Gandhian ideals of non-violence?

solution_steps.action: Analyze local peasant and tribal protests
solution_steps.explain: In Kheda, peasants protested high land revenue; in Guntur, tribals held forest satyagrahas against grazing restrictions; in Punjab, Sikhs sought to remove corrupt mahants.

solution_steps.action: Explain the popular perception of Gandhiji
solution_steps.explain: People often viewed Gandhiji as a messiah who would end taxes and evictions, sometimes taking actions in his name that did not align with his strict non-violent principles.

concepts.title: The Happenings of 1922-1929 and Purna Swaraj
concepts.definition: The period of transition marked by the withdrawal of Non-Cooperation after the Chauri Chaura incident, constructive work, the Simon Commission boycott, and the resolution for complete independence.
concepts.key_idea: The decade of the 1920s concluded with the Congress resolving to fight for Purna Swaraj (complete independence) under Jawaharlal Nehru.
question_patterns: Why did Mahatma Gandhi call off the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922?
What was the Chauri Chaura incident?
Why did Indians boycott the Simon Commission in 1927?
When and under whose presidency did the Congress resolve to fight for Purna Swaraj?
What was the significance of January 26, 1930?

solution_steps.action: Explain the withdrawal of Non-Cooperation
solution_steps.explain: In February 1922, Gandhiji called off the movement after a violent crowd set fire to a police station in Chauri Chaura, killing 22 policemen.

solution_steps.action: Outline the path to Purna Swaraj
solution_steps.explain: Following constructive work, protests against the all-white Simon Commission in 1927, and revolutionary activities, the Congress resolved for Purna Swaraj in 1929, observing Independence Day on 26 January 1930.

concepts.title: The Dandi March and the Civil Disobedience Movement
concepts.definition: The historic 240-mile march led by Gandhiji in 1930 to break the British salt monopoly, launching a nationwide Civil Disobedience campaign with massive participation, including women.
concepts.key_idea: Breaking the salt law united diverse social groups against a basic shared grievance and mobilized women on a large scale.
question_patterns: Why did Gandhiji choose to break the salt law as a method of protest?
Describe the route and details of the Dandi March of 1930.
How did women participate in the Salt Satyagraha?
Who was Ambabai and what was her contribution to the freedom struggle?
What were the political outcomes of the Civil Disobedience Movement and the Government of India Act of 1935?

solution_steps.action: Explain the choice of salt as a symbol
solution_steps.explain: Salt was an essential food item taxed by the state monopoly; breaking this law united the rich and poor against colonial rule.

solution_steps.action: Describe the march and its impact
solution_steps.explain: Gandhiji and his followers marched 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi to make salt. This led to the Government of India Act of 1935, which prescribed provincial autonomy and led to elections in 1937.

concepts.title: The Quit India Movement and the Path to Partition
concepts.definition: The final phase of the freedom struggle launched in 1942 during World War II, followed by negotiations, communal riots, and the eventual partition of the subcontinent in 1947.
concepts.key_idea: The 'Do or Die' call of Quit India and the failure of negotiations led to independence accompanied by the tragedy of Partition.
question_patterns: What was the slogan given by Gandhiji during the Quit India movement?
How did the British respond to the Quit India movement of 1942?
Why did the negotiations between the Congress, the Muslim League, and the British fail after World War II?
What was the significance of the Cabinet Mission of 1946?
Describe the events that led to the creation of Pakistan and the violence of Partition.

solution_steps.action: Explain the Quit India Movement
solution_steps.explain: In 1942, Gandhiji launched the Quit India movement with the slogan 'Do or Die'. Despite severe British repression, the movement spread rapidly among youth and peasants.

solution_steps.action: Trace the developments leading to Partition
solution_steps.explain: The Muslim League demanded independent states in 1940. Following the failure of the 1946 Cabinet Mission and the League's call for 'Direct Action Day' on 16 August 1946, widespread riots made Partition inevitable in 1947.

solution_template.explain: In Kheda, peasants protested high land revenue; in Guntur, tribals held forest satyagrahas against grazing restrictions; in Punjab, Sikhs sought to remove corrupt mahants.

solution_template.action: Explain the popular perception of Gandhiji
solution_template.explain: People often viewed Gandhiji as a messiah who would end taxes and evictions, sometimes taking actions in his name that did not align with his strict non-violent principles.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why did Mahatma Gandhi call off the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922?

solution_template.action: Explain the withdrawal of Non-Cooperation
solution_template.explain: In February 1922, Gandhiji called off the movement after a violent crowd set fire to a police station in Chauri Chaura, killing 22 policemen.

solution_template.action: Outline the path to Purna Swaraj
solution_template.explain: Following constructive work, protests against the all-white Simon Commission in 1927, and revolutionary activities, the Congress resolved for Purna Swaraj in 1929, observing Independence Day on 26 January 1930.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why did Gandhiji choose to break the salt law as a method of protest?

solution_template.action: Explain the choice of salt as a symbol
solution_template.explain: Salt was an essential food item taxed by the state monopoly; breaking this law united the rich and poor against colonial rule.

solution_template.action: Describe the march and its impact
solution_template.explain: Gandhiji and his followers marched 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi to make salt. This led to the Government of India Act of 1935, which prescribed provincial autonomy and led to elections in 1937.

worked_examples.question_pattern: What was the slogan given by Gandhiji during the Quit India movement?

solution_template.action: Explain the Quit India Movement
solution_template.explain: In 1942, Gandhiji launched the Quit India movement with the slogan 'Do or Die'. Despite severe British repression, the movement spread rapidly among youth and peasants.

solution_template.action: Trace the developments leading to Partition
solution_template.explain: The Muslim League demanded independent states in 1940. Following the failure of the 1946 Cabinet Mission and the League's call for 'Direct Action Day' on 16 August 1946, widespread riots made Partition inevitable in 1947.
